{{Short description|Variant Fourier transforms}}
[[File:Sine and cosine transforms with inversion equations together.svg|thumb|The sine and cosine transforms convert a function into a [[frequency domain]] representation as a sum of [[Sine wave|sine and cosine waves]]. The inverse transform converts back to a [[time]] or [[Space|spatial]] domain.]] 

In [[mathematics]], the Fourier '''sine and cosine transforms''' are [[integral equations]] that decompose arbitrary functions into a sum of [[sine waves]] representing the [[Even and odd functions#Even–odd decomposition|odd component]] of the function plus cosine waves representing the even component of the function. The modern, [[complex number|complex-valued]] [[Fourier transform]] concisely [[Sine and cosine transforms#Relation with complex exponentials|contains]] both the sine and cosine transforms. Since the sine and cosine transforms use sine and cosine waves instead of [[Euler's formula#Relationship to trigonometry|complex exponentials]] and don't require [[complex number]]s or [[negative frequency]], they more closely correspond to [[Joseph Fourier]]'s original transform equations and are still preferred in some [[signal processing]] and [[statistical]] applications and may be better suited as an introduction to [[Fourier analysis]]. 

==Definition==
[[File:Fourier_transform_time_and_frequency_domains_(small).gif|right|thumb|Fourier transforms relate a time-domain function (red) to a frequency-domain function (blue). Sine or cosine waves that make up the original function will appear as peaks in the frequency domain functions produced by the sine or cosine transform, respectively.]]
The '''Fourier sine transform''' of <math>f(t)</math> is:{{NoteTag|The sine transform is sometimes denoted with <math>{\mathcal F}_s (f)</math> instead of <math>{\hat f}^s</math>.}}
{{Equation box 1|border|title=Fourier sine transform|indent=:|cellpadding=6|border colour=#0073CF|background colour=#F5FFFA|equation=<math>{\hat f}^s(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(t)\sin(2\pi \xi t) \,dt.</math>}}If <math>t</math> means [[time]], then <math>\xi</math> is [[frequency]] in cycles per unit time,{{NoteTag|While this article uses ordinary frequency for <math>\xi</math> in cycles per unit time, which typically uses the [[Hertz]] and the [[second]] as units, these transforms are sometimes expressed using [[angular frequency]] in angular units (e.g. [[radians]]) per unit time, where <math>\omega</math>{{nbsp}}[[radians per second]] equals <math>2\pi\xi</math>.}} but in the abstract, they can be any dual pair of variables (e.g. [[Position (geometry)|position]] and [[spatial frequency]]).

The sine transform is necessarily an [[odd function]] of frequency, i.e. for all <math>\xi</math>:
<math display="block">  {\hat f}^s(-\xi) = - {\hat f}^s(\xi).</math>[[File:Sinc-ax.svg|thumb|The cosine transform of a simple [[rectangular function]] (of height <math>\tfrac{1}{a}</math> and width <math>a</math>) is the [[Normalized sinc function|normalized sinc]]<math>(a \xi)</math> plotted above.]]


The '''Fourier cosine transform''' of <math>f(t)</math> is:{{NoteTag|The cosine transform is sometimes denoted with <math>{\mathcal F}_c (f)</math> instead of <math>{\hat f}^c</math>.}}
{{Equation box 1|border|title=Fourier cosine transform|indent=:|cellpadding=6|border colour=#0073CF|background colour=#F5FFFA|equation=<math>{\hat f}^c(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(t)\cos(2\pi \xi t) \,dt.</math>}}The cosine transform is necessarily an [[even function]] of frequency, i.e. for all <math>\xi</math>:
<math display="block">{\hat f}^c(-\xi) =  {\hat f}^c(\xi).</math>

=== Odd and even simplification ===
[[File:Gaussian that is own cosine transform alpha-is-pi.png|thumb|Like all even functions, the left half of a [[Gaussian function]] is a mirror image of its right half and its sine transform is entirely 0. Gaussians have the form <math>e^{-\alpha t^2}</math> and their cosine transform:
{{br}}
<math display="block">{\hat f}^c(\xi) = \sqrt{\tfrac{\pi}{\alpha}}\, e^{-\frac{(\pi \xi)^2}{\alpha}}</math>
{{br}}
also is a Gaussian. The plotted Gaussian uses {{math|1=''α''=''π''}} and is its own cosine transform.]]

The [[Even and odd functions#Multiplication and division|multiplication rules for even and odd functions]] shown in the overbraces in the following equations dramatically simplify the integrands when transforming [[even and odd functions]]. Some authors<ref>[[Mary L. Boas]], ''[[Mathematical Methods in the Physical Sciences]]'', 2nd Ed, John Wiley & Sons Inc, 1983. {{ISBN|0-471-04409-1}}</ref> even only define the cosine transform for even functions <math> f_\text{even}(t)</math>. Since cosine is an even function and because the integral of an even function from <math> {-} \infty</math> to <math> \infty</math> [[Even and odd functions#Basic analytic properties|is twice its integral]] from <math> 0</math> to <math> \infty</math>, the cosine transform of any even function can be simplified to avoid negative <math>t</math>:

<math display="block"> {\hat f}^c(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \overbrace{f_\text{even}(t) \cdot \cos(2\pi \xi t)}^\text{even·even=even} \, dt = 2 \int_0^\infty f_\text{even}(t)\cos(2\pi \xi t) \, dt.</math>

And because the integral from <math> {-} \infty</math> to <math> \infty</math> of [[Even and odd functions#Basic analytic properties|any odd function is zero]], the cosine transform of any odd function is simply zero:

<math display="block"> {\hat f}^c(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \overbrace{f_\text{odd}(t) \cdot \cos(2\pi \xi t)}^\text{odd·even=odd} \, dt = 0.</math>

[[File:Sine-transform-of-sine-of-ax-is-two-odd-symmetrical-Dirac-deltas.png|thumb|Odd functions are unchanged if [[Rotation (mathematics)|rotated]] 180 [[Degree (angle)|degrees]] about the [[Origin (mathematics)|origin]]. Their cosine transform is entirely zero. The above odd function contains two half-sized [[Dirac delta function#Translation|time-shifted Dirac delta functions]]. Its sine transform is simply <math>\sin(a\xi).</math> Likewise, the sine transform of <math>\sin(a\xi)</math> is the above plot. Thus, the sine wave function and the time-shifted Dirac delta function form a ''transform pair''.]]

Similarly, because sin is odd, the sine transform of any odd function <math>f_\text{odd}(t)</math> also simplifies to avoid negative <math>t</math>:

<math display="block">{\hat f}^s(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \overbrace{f_\text{odd}(t) \cdot \sin(2\pi \xi t) }^\text{odd·odd=even} \, dt = 2\int_0^\infty f_\text{odd}(t)\sin(2\pi \xi t) \, dt</math>

and the sine transform of any even function is simply zero:

<math display="block">  {\hat f}^s(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \overbrace{f_\text{even}(t) \cdot \sin(2\pi \xi t)}^\text{even·odd=odd} \, dt = 0.</math>

The sine transform represents the [[Even and odd functions#Even–odd decomposition|odd part of a function]], while the cosine transform represents the even part of a function.

=== Other conventions ===
Just like the Fourier transform takes the form of different equations with different constant factors (see {{Section link|Fourier transform|Unitarity and definition for square integrable functions}} for discussion), other authors also define the cosine transform as<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nyack |first=Cuthbert |date=1996 |title=Fourier Transform, Cosine and Sine Transforms |url=https://cnyack.homestead.com/files/afourtr/ftcosin.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230607155213/https://cnyack.homestead.com/files/afourtr/ftcosin.htm |archive-date=2023-06-07 |access-date=2018-10-08 |website=cnyack.homestead.com}}</ref>
<math display="block"> {\hat f}^c(\xi)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \int_0^\infty f(t)\cos(2\pi \xi t) \,dt</math>
and the sine transform as
<math display="block"> {\hat f}^s(\xi) =\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \int_0^\infty f(t)\sin(2\pi \xi t) \,dt.</math>Another convention defines the cosine transform as<ref>{{Cite book | last=Coleman | first=Matthew P. | title=An Introduction to Partial Differential Equations with MATLAB | date=2013 | isbn=978-1-4398-9846-8 | edition=Second | location=Boca Raton | pages=221 | oclc=822959644}}</ref> <math display="block">F_c(\alpha) = \frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^\infty f(x) \cos(\alpha x) \, dx</math> and the sine transform as <math display="block">F_s(\alpha) = \frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^\infty f(x) \sin(\alpha x) \, dx</math>using <math>\alpha</math> as the transformation variable. And while <math>t</math> is typically used to represent the [[time domain]], <math>x</math> is often instead used to represent a spatial domain when transforming to spatial frequencies.

==Fourier inversion==
The original function <math>f</math> can be recovered from its sine and cosine transforms under the usual hypotheses{{NoteTag|The usual hypotheses are that <math>f</math> and both of its transforms should be absolutely integrable. For more details on the different hypotheses, see [[Fourier inversion theorem]].}} using the inversion formula:<ref>{{cite book|last=Poincaré|first=Henri|authorlink=Henri Poincaré|title=Theorie analytique de la propagation de la chaleur| year=1895|publisher=G. Carré|location=Paris|pages= 108ff|url=http://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k5500702f/f115.image}}</ref>
{{Equation box 1|border|title=Fourier inversion (from the sine and cosine transforms)|indent=:|cellpadding=6|border colour=#0073CF|background colour=#F5FFFA|equation=<math>f(t) = \underbrace{ \int _{-\infty}^\infty {\hat f}^s(\xi) \sin (2\pi \xi t) \,d\xi}_{\text{odd component of } f(t)} \, + \underbrace{ \int _{-\infty}^\infty {\hat f}^c(\xi) \cos (2\pi \xi t) \,d\xi}_{\text{even component of } f(t)} \, .</math>}}

=== Simplifications ===
Note that since both integrands are even functions of <math>\xi</math>, the concept of negative frequency can be avoided by doubling the result of integrating over non-negative frequencies:

<math display="block">f(t) = 2 \int _{0}^\infty {\hat f}^s(\xi) \sin (2\pi \xi t) \,d\xi \, + 2 \int _{0}^\infty {\hat f}^c(\xi) \cos (2\pi \xi t) \,d\xi \, .</math>

Also, if <math>f</math> is an [[odd function]], then the cosine transform is zero, so its inversion simplifies to:<math display="block">f(t) = \int _{-\infty}^\infty {\hat f}^s(\xi) \sin (2\pi \xi t) \, d\xi , \text{ only if }f(t)\text{ is odd.}</math>

Likewise, if the original function <math>f</math> is an [[even function]], then the sine transform is zero, so its inversion also simplifies to:

<math display="block">f(t) = \int _{-\infty}^\infty {\hat f}^c(\xi) \cos (2\pi \xi t) \, d\xi , \text{ only if }f(t)\text{ is even.}</math>

Remarkably, these last two simplified inversion formulas look identical to the original sine and cosine transforms, respectively, though with <math>t</math> swapped with <math>\xi</math> (and with <math>f</math> swapped with <math>{\hat f}^s</math> or <math>{\hat f}^c</math>). A consequence of this symmetry is that their inversion and transform processes still work when the two functions are swapped. Two such functions are called ''transform pairs''.{{NoteTag|The more general modern [[Fourier transform]] has this symmetry even when the original functions aren't even or odd. A notation to denote Fourier transform pairs is <math>f(t)\ \stackrel{\mathcal{F}}{\longleftrightarrow}\ \widehat f(\xi).</math>}}

=== Overview of inversion proof ===
Using the addition formula for [[cosine]], the full inversion formula can also be rewritten as ''Fourier's integral formula'':<ref>{{citation|author=Edwin Titchmarsh|title=Introduction to the theory of the Fourier integral|publisher=Oxford at the Clarendon Press|year=1948|page=1}}</ref><ref name="Whittaker-Watson_1927">{{cite book |title=A Course Of Modern Analysis: An Introduction to the General Theory of Infinite Processes and of Analytic Functions; with an Account of the Principal Transcendental Functions |author-last1=Whittaker |author-first1=Edmund Taylor |author-link1=Edmund Taylor Whittaker |author-last2=Watson |author-first2=George Neville |author-link2=George Neville Watson |date=1927-01-02 |edition=4th |publisher=Cambridge University Press |publication-place=Cambridge, UK |page=189|isbn=0-521-06794-4 |id={{ISBN|978-0-521-06794-2}}}} </ref>
<math display="block">f(t) = \int _{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty  f(x) \cos (2\pi\xi (x-t) ) \,dx\,d\xi.</math>
This theorem is often stated under different hypotheses, that <math>f</math> is integrable, and is of [[bounded variation]] on an open interval containing the point <math>t</math>, in which case
<math display="block"> \tfrac12\lim_{h\to 0}\left(f(t+h)+f(t-h)\right) = 2\int_0^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty  f(x) \cos (2\pi\xi (x-t) ) \,dx\,d\xi. </math>

This latter form is a useful intermediate step in proving the inverse formulae for the since and cosine transforms.  One method of deriving it, due to [[Cauchy]] is to insert a <math>e^{-\delta\xi}</math> into the integral, where <math>\delta > 0</math> is fixed.  Then
<math display="block">2\int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_0^\infty e^{-\delta\xi}\cos(2\pi\xi(x-t))\,d\xi\, f(x)\,dx = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\frac{2\delta}{\delta^2+4\pi^2(x-t)^2}\,dx.</math>
Now when <math>\delta\to 0</math>, the integrand tends to zero except at <math>x=t</math>, so that formally the above is
<math display="block">f(t)\int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{2\delta}{\delta^2+4\pi^2(x-t)^2}\,dx = f(t).</math>

==Relation with complex exponentials==
The complex exponential form of the [[Fourier transform]] used more often today is<ref>{{Cite web |last=Valentinuzzi |first=Max E. |date=2016-01-25 |title=Highlights in the History of the Fourier Transform |url=https://www.embs.org/pulse/articles/highlights-in-the-history-of-the-fourier-transform/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240515224625/https://www.embs.org/pulse/articles/highlights-in-the-history-of-the-fourier-transform/ |archive-date=2024-05-15 |access-date=2024-09-09 |website=[[IEEE Pulse]] |language=en-US}}</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\hat{f}(\xi) &= \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(t) e^{-2\pi i\xi t}\,dt \\
\end{align} \,</math>where <math>i</math> is the [[square root of negative one]]. By applying [[Euler's formula]] <math display="inline">(e^{i x} = \cos x + i \sin x) , </math> it can be shown (for real-valued functions) that the Fourier transform's real component is the cosine transform (representing the even component of the original function) and the Fourier transform's imaginary component is the negative of the sine transform (representing the odd component of the original function):<ref>{{Cite web |last=Williams |first=Lance R. |date=2011-09-06 |title=Even and odd functions |url=https://www.cs.unm.edu/~williams/cs530/symmetry.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240502192745/https://www.cs.unm.edu/~williams/cs530/symmetry.pdf |archive-date=2024-05-02 |access-date=2024-09-11 |website=www.cs.unm.edu/~williams/}}</ref><math display="block">\begin{align}
\hat{f}(\xi) &= \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(t) \left(\cos (2\pi\xi t) - i\,\sin (2\pi\xi t)\right) dt && \text{Euler's Formula} \\
&= \left (\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(t)\cos(2\pi \xi t) \,dt \right ) - i \left (\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(t)\sin(2\pi \xi t) \,dt \right ) \\
&= {\hat f}^c (\xi) - i \, {\hat f}^s (\xi) \, .
\end{align}</math>Because of this relationship, the cosine transform of functions whose Fourier transform is known (e.g. in {{Slink|Fourier transform|Tables of important Fourier transforms}}) can be simply found by taking the real part of the Fourier transform:<math display="block"> {\hat f}^c(\xi) = \mathrm{Re} {[ \; {\hat f}(\xi) \; ]}</math>while the sine transform is simply the ''negative'' of the imaginary part of the Fourier transform:<math display="block"> {\hat f}^s(\xi) = - \mathrm{Im} {[ \; {\hat f}(\xi) \; ]} \, . </math>

=== Pros and cons ===
[[File:Sine cosine and the sum over one period.svg|thumb|Adding a sine wave (red) and a cosine wave (blue) of the same frequency results a [[Phase (waves)#Phase shift|phase-shifted]] sine wave (green) of that [[List of trigonometric identities#Sine and cosine|same frequency, but whose amplitude and phase depends on the amplitudes of the original sine and cosine wave]]. Hence, at a particular frequency, the sine transform and the cosine transform ''together'' essentially only represent one sine wave that could have any phase shift.]]

An advantage of the modern Fourier transform is that while the sine and cosine transforms together are required to extract the [[Phase (waves)|phase]] information of a frequency, the modern Fourier transform instead compactly packs both phase ''and'' amplitude information inside its complex valued result. But a disadvantage is its requirement on understanding complex numbers, complex exponentials, and negative frequency.

The sine and cosine transforms meanwhile have the advantage that all quantities are real. Since positive frequencies can fully express them, the non-trivial concept of [[negative frequency]] needed in the regular Fourier transform can be avoided. They may also be convenient when the original function is already even or odd or can be made even or odd, in which case only the cosine or the sine transform respectively is needed. For instance, even though an input may not be even or odd, a [[discrete cosine transform]] may start by [[:File:DCT-symmetries.svg|assuming an even extension]] of its input while a [[discrete sine transform]] may start by [[:File:DST-symmetries.svg|assuming an odd extension]] of its input, to avoid having to compute the entire [[discrete Fourier transform]].

== Numerical evaluation ==
Using standard methods of numerical evaluation for Fourier integrals, such as Gaussian or [[tanh-sinh quadrature]], is likely to lead to completely incorrect results, as the quadrature sum is (for most integrands of interest) highly ill-conditioned.
Special numerical methods which exploit the structure of the oscillation are required, an example of which is Ooura's method for Fourier integrals<ref>Takuya Ooura, Masatake Mori, ''A robust double exponential formula for Fourier-type integrals'', Journal of computational and applied mathematics 112.1-2 (1999): 229-241.</ref> This method attempts to evaluate the integrand at locations which asymptotically approach the zeros of the oscillation (either the sine or cosine), quickly reducing the magnitude of positive and negative terms which are summed.
